title: Ten papers that built computing
tagline: Eight decades of ideas that other ideas were built on top of. Spacing is ordinal — the rail names the real gap between entries so the sequence stays readable.

events.title: On Computable Numbers
events.summary: Defines a machine simple enough to reason about and general enough to compute anything computable — then shows what it still cannot do.
keyPoints: A machine is a finite state table, a head, and an unbounded tape — nothing else is needed.
A universal machine can simulate any other machine given its description, which is the idea of software.
The halting problem has no general solution, so some questions about programs are permanently out of reach.
Written to answer Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem, not to design a computer.
events.impact: Every model of computation since has been measured against this one, and every 'this cannot be automated' argument in the field traces back to its diagonal argument. It also gave the industry its central abstraction: a program is data.

resources.label: On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem

events.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
events.summary: Separates the meaning of a message from the problem of moving it, and gives the second one an exact mathematics.
keyPoints: Information is measured as reduction in uncertainty — the entropy of the source, in bits.
Every noisy channel has a capacity, and below it arbitrarily reliable transmission is possible.
Source coding and channel coding are separable problems, which is why compression and error correction are different layers.
The engineering problem is reproducing a message, not understanding it.
events.impact: Compression, error-correcting codes, modems, storage density, and the entire notion of a 'bit' as a unit come from this paper. It is also the reason cross-entropy is the default loss function in machine learning.

resources.label: Performance reasoning on data platforms
resources.note: Where information-theoretic limits show up in practice

events.title: Three Models for the Description of Language
events.summary: Ranks grammars by the machinery they need, producing the hierarchy that still decides how every parser is built.
keyPoints: Finite-state models cannot capture nested structure; context-free grammars can.
Grammar classes form a strict hierarchy, each requiring strictly more machine.
Structure is generated by rules, not by statistics over surface strings.
The argument was about natural language, and computing took the tools.
events.impact: Regular expressions, lexers, LR and LL parsers, and the reason JSON and YAML need different machinery than a regex all descend from this classification.

resources.label: Three Models for the Description of Language
SQL regex and pattern reasoning
resources.note: Where finite-state matching hits its ceiling

events.title: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks
events.summary: Argues that applications should ask for data by its content, not by walking the pointers whoever stored it happened to choose.
keyPoints: Data is a set of relations; order and physical layout are not part of the meaning.
Physical data independence: storage can change without rewriting applications.
Relational algebra gives queries a closed, composable semantics.
Normalisation removes the update anomalies that hierarchical stores lived with.
events.impact: Declarative querying became the default interface to data. Half a century later the query optimiser — the direct consequence of not specifying access paths — is still the most valuable component in a data platform.

resources.label: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks
Choosing a data platform by workload

events.title: SEQUEL
events.summary: A structured English query language over Codd's algebra — the syntax that became SQL.

resources.label: SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language

events.title: System R
events.summary: The first working relational engine, and with it the cost-based optimiser.

resources.label: System R: Relational Approach to Database Management

events.title: SQL becomes a standard
events.summary: One query language across competing vendors — portability as a market force.

events.title: MapReduce
events.summary: Declarative data processing escapes the single database and lands on commodity clusters.

resources.label: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters

events.title: Dynamo
events.summary: Trades the relational contract for availability, and starts the NoSQL decade.

resources.label: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store

events.title: Spanner
events.summary: Global scale and SQL semantics at once — the pendulum swings back to Codd.

events.title: Lakehouse
events.summary: Transactions and schema return to the data lake; the table is once again the interface.

resources.label: Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms
Choosing a data platform by workload

events.title: The Complexity of Theorem-Proving Procedures
events.summary: Shows that one problem is at least as hard as every problem whose answers are easy to check.
keyPoints: Satisfiability is NP-complete: every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time.
Hardness becomes a structural property of a problem, not a comment on one algorithm.
P versus NP is stated as the question the field still cannot answer.
Karp's 1972 paper turned the single result into a map of twenty-one hard problems.
events.impact: Gave engineers a way to say 'this is hard for a reason' and move on to approximation, heuristics, or a reformulation — and gave cryptography its working assumption.

events.title: A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication
events.byline: Vinton G. Cerf & Robert E. Kahn
events.summary: Describes how independently run networks can carry each other's traffic without agreeing on how they work inside.

media.alt: Packet motif for the 1974 TCP paper

keyPoints: Gateways translate between networks; neither network has to change.
Reliability is the hosts' job, not the network's — the end-to-end argument in embryo.
A common address format and a common datagram make the federation possible.
TCP and IP were one protocol here and were split apart later.
events.impact: This is the internet's architecture. The decision to keep the network simple and push function to the edges is why the same substrate carried file transfer, the web, video, and everything since without redesign.

resources.label: A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication

events.title: New Directions in Cryptography
events.summary: Two parties who have never met, talking over a line everyone can hear, end up sharing a secret.
keyPoints: Public-key cryptography removes the need for a pre-shared secret channel.
Key exchange over a public channel is possible using one-way functions.
Digital signatures are introduced as the authentication half of the idea.
Security is grounded in computational hardness rather than secrecy of the method.
events.impact: TLS, SSH, signed software updates, certificate authorities, and every online payment rest on this. It also made cryptography a public research field rather than a government one.

events.title: Information Management: A Proposal
events.summary: An internal CERN memo proposing linked documents with no central index — and a supervisor's note reading 'vague but exciting'.

media.alt: Linked-documents motif for the 1989 web proposal

keyPoints: Links point outward without permission and without a registry.
Broken links are accepted as the price of decentralisation.
Documents are addressed by location, and the format is separate from the transport.
The proposal is about surviving staff turnover at a physics lab, not about publishing.
events.impact: URLs, HTTP, and HTML followed within two years. The choice to tolerate broken links is the reason the web could grow without anyone's approval.

events.title: WorldWideWeb ships
events.summary: The first browser, the first server, and the first page, all on one NeXT machine.

events.title: Mosaic
events.summary: Inline images and an installer — the web stops being a physics tool.

events.title: W3C founded
events.summary: Standards move to a neutral body before the browser vendors fork the format.

events.title: REST
events.summary: Names the architectural style the web already had, and hands it to API designers.

resources.label: Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures

events.title: HTTP/2
events.summary: Multiplexing and header compression, without changing what a URL means.

events.title: The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine
events.summary: Treats a link as a vote, and ranks the whole web by who is voted for by pages that are themselves voted for.

media.alt: Ranking motif for the 1998 PageRank paper

keyPoints: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random surfer over the link graph.
Anchor text describes the target better than the target often describes itself.
Relevance is computed from structure, which is much harder to fake than page content.
The paper also describes the crawler, index, and storage — it is a systems paper as much as a ranking one.
events.impact: Made the web navigable, funded a decade of infrastructure research, and established link-graph eigenvector methods as a general tool for ranking anything with references.

resources.label: The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine

events.title: Attention Is All You Need
events.byline: Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser & Polosukhin
events.summary: Removes recurrence from sequence modelling entirely, leaving an architecture that scales with the hardware it runs on.

media.alt: Attention-matrix motif for the 2017 Transformer paper

keyPoints: Self-attention relates every position to every other in one step, so path length is constant.
Dropping recurrence makes training parallel across the sequence, not just the batch.
Multi-head attention lets one layer attend to several relationships at once.
Positional encodings restore the order that attention alone discards.
events.impact: The architecture behind essentially every large language model, and since adopted for vision, audio, and protein structure. Its real contribution was making sequence models scale with compute, which turned a research direction into an industry.

events.title: BERT
events.summary: Bidirectional pre-training, then fine-tuning — one model per task becomes one model, then a task.

resources.label: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers

events.title: Scaling laws
events.summary: Loss falls as a power law in compute, data, and parameters — capability becomes a budgeting question.

resources.label: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

events.title: GPT-3
events.summary: In-context learning: the prompt, not the gradient, specifies the task.

events.title: InstructGPT
events.summary: Alignment from human feedback turns a text predictor into something that follows instructions.

resources.label: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

events.title: Chinchilla
events.summary: Corrects the scaling recipe: most large models were badly under-trained on data.
